h: London's restraint is no yardstick: the right to gather is our own
dek: Pankhuri Agarwal, a lecturer at King's College London, argues that comparing India with London, where people waving the tricolour faced no action, is dangerous, because it makes the restraint of the old colonial power the measure of Indian freedom.
body: In October, hundreds of Indians at India House and Parliament Square in London demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and went home peacefully. Then a comparison began to circulate: no one was arrested in Britain for waving the tricolour, while at home young people are going to jail for the same thing. According to Pankhuri Agarwal, who teaches at King's College London, the comparison is moving but leads to the wrong conclusion.

She argues that the difference is less about tolerance and more about the target. No British minister's future depends on India's voter rolls, while in Delhi people are questioning the very people who also control the police. In the background is the allegation that more than 13 crore names were cut, and in the capital, closed metro stations, internet shutdowns and, according to a Home Ministry official, more than 2,000 detentions.

Agarwal recalls the history: imprisonment without trial under the Rowlatt Act, Section 144 restrictions, and Jallianwala Bagh, where bullets lay beneath the claim of 'order'. In the 1923 Nagpur Flag Satyagraha, volunteers were arrested for the right to march with the flag. The fight was not over a piece of cloth but over gathering in a public place.

According to the writer, the Constitution gave the right of assembly, but the tools of restriction survived: Section 144 was imposed during the CAA protests, it is now Section 163 of the BNSS, and now Jantar Mantar has lost its status as a protest site. In 2023 the Supreme Court put the Chief Justice on the panel that selects the commissioners, but Parliament replaced him with a Union minister. Removing a commissioner is as hard as impeachment, so public pressure is the only path left.

Agarwal says opinions may differ on whether Gyanesh Kumar should go, but demanding a resignation is a legitimate way of asking an institution for answers. This right is neither London's favour nor Delhi's. Her conclusion: a government confident of its own legitimacy does not need to turn its capital into a fortress.
nazar: This article breaks the easy comfort that 'there, at least, there is freedom'. The real question is how much of the right written into our own Constitution survives on the ground. When protest sites are pushed to the edges of the city and detention becomes routine, the first voices silenced are those with neither lawyers nor platforms: workers, students, Muslims, Dalits and Adivasis.
sawal: Since when did asking questions in our own capital become a crime?
ref: Flag Satyagraha (1923)
In Nagpur and Jabalpur, Congress volunteers broke a British ban on marching with the national flag. Hundreds were arrested under Sardar Patel's leadership.
BNSS Section 163
The section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita that replaced the old Section 144. It lets magistrates ban gatherings in an area.
ank: Alleged: names cut in the revision
photo_note: Representative image: the Jantar Mantar observatory

h: The noise about a 'foreign hand', and the foreign money no one mentions
dek: Archbishop Joseph D'Souza argues that those in power who call young anti-SIR protesters foreign agents stay silent about the foreign money that reaches them and those close to them.
body: On 10 October, BJP president Nitin Nabin said the protests against the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls were happening at the behest of 'foreign forces'. According to Joseph D'Souza, president of the All India Christian Council, this is an old trick: call the critic a puppet, and you no longer need to answer the complaint.

The writer traces its roots to Indira Gandhi's time, when students in Gujarat and Bihar, JP's supporters and trade unions were accused of foreign influence, and in the end the Emergency came. The Jana Sangh too was a target then. After Graham Staines and his two sons were murdered in Odisha in 1999, there was talk of an 'international conspiracy', which the Home Ministry later told Parliament was baseless.

D'Souza says that most of the nearly 13 crore people whose names are alleged to have been cut today are poor and from minorities, and those on the streets have come not on anyone's orders but to ask for their vote back. Then he turns the question around: according to a Bellingcat investigation, two American organisations linked to the Sangh received 117.8 million dollars between 2020 and 2024, a large part of which came to India. Why did no leader see a 'foreign hand' in this?

The writer recalls the Vedanta case, in which the Delhi High Court in 2014 found both the BJP and the Congress guilty of breaking the FCRA. In his account, the response was to change the law itself, through the Finance Acts of 2016 and then 2018, and with effect from 1976 at that. The same law is used to cancel the licences of churches, schools and thousands of organisations. Foreign investment flowing into big business houses is called 'confidence', while a grant to a school for Dalit children is called a 'threat'.

His conclusion is that the 'foreign hand' has become the oldest refuge of the class in power, and 79 years after independence, Indians do not need an outsider to tell them that their vote has been taken away.
nazar: This article points to a concrete double standard. The 'foreign hand' charge is really a way of changing the debate: the question was about the voter roll, and the answer became a test of patriotism. It hits hardest at the small organisations that work among Dalits, Adivasis and minorities, whose licence can be cancelled with a single signature.
sawal: Whose foreign money is treason, and whose is investment?
ref: FCRA
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, which controls foreign donations to institutions and organisations. Thousands of NGOs have had their licences cancelled under it.
Bellingcat
An international journalism group that investigates using open sources, working from documents, photographs and public records.

h: A pardon after the hanging: appeals of struck-off voters race the election clock
dek: In The Leaflet, three writers argue that during the SIR, Form 6 was changed without changing the rules, and appeals by struck-off voters are so slow that relief arrives after the election.
by: Abdullah Ghazali, Asif Iqbal, Madhav Anand
body: According to the writers, about 13 crore names were removed from the draft rolls in the revision, and a Lokniti-CSDS survey showed an unprecedented fall in the Election Commission's credibility. Yet in 2001 President K.R. Narayanan had said that the people placed the Commission even above the judiciary.

The first question is about Form 6. This form is laid down in the Registration of Electors Rules of 1960, which the central government makes, and under the 1978 Mohinder Singh Gill judgment, where rules exist the Commission must act within them. Even so, in July a new question was added to the online Form 6: whether the applicant, their parents or grandparents were on the last intensive roll, and the rules were not amended at all. It is alleged that one election commissioner himself called this illegal.

The second question is about appeals. In West Bengal, appellate tribunals were set up just five weeks before the election, and the roll cannot be changed after nominations close. By mid-May, only about 6,500 of nearly 25 lakh appeals had been decided, and 61 per cent of those people were restored. The writers say this means many of those denied a vote in April were in fact entitled to it. By September, the Commission itself had filed more than 20 lakh appeals against names that judicial officers had already found valid.

It did not stop at the vote. According to the writers, in Bengal orders came to treat those left off the roll as ineligible for welfare schemes and to stop their ration cards, although the Food Security Act sets no condition of citizenship or registration for rations. Someone whose home changed did not stop being hungry.

The article ends with Gandhi's 1924 words in 'Young India': cutting names before an election and adding them afterwards is like sending a pardon after the hanging. The writers argue that if relief comes only after the election has passed, it is exactly that pardon.
nazar: The strength of this article is in its numbers: where appeals were heard, most people turned out to be right. So the problem is not the exceptions but the structure. For those who could not file an appeal, the poorest, migrants and the less educated, their rations were put at stake along with their vote.
sawal: What use is a vote returned after the election?
ref: Form 6
The application form to become a new voter or to have a name added again. Its format is set by the central government under the Registration of Electors Rules of 1960.
Mohinder Singh Gill judgment (1978)
A Supreme Court ruling that the Election Commission's powers are wide, but where a law or rules exist, the Commission must work according to them.

h: A former election officer warns: defending the Commission is now costing the BJP
dek: Former IAS officer K.B.S. Sidhu, who has served as a district election officer and a Commission observer, argues that the SIR's 'mapping' conditions are irrational and illegal, and that defending the Chief Election Commissioner is backfiring on the ruling party.
body: Former IAS officer K.B.S. Sidhu has worked at every level, from the polling booth to district election officer of Amritsar and Commission observer in three Lok Sabha elections. In this piece, written after a TV debate on 12 October, he describes that week: locks on Jantar Mantar, its status as a protest site ended, and a Sunday sitting of the Supreme Court that reaffirmed the right to peaceful assembly.

His basic point is simple: there are only three conditions for becoming a voter, citizenship, age 18, and ordinary residence in that area. Article 326 treats the vote as a right, not a gift from the government. So the Commission's 'mapping' conditions, that is, finding one's own or one's parents' name on an old roll, are in his view irrational and illegal. The figure of 33 lakh 'unmapped' voters in Delhi itself shows that the exercise is flawed.

Sidhu also says that Article 324 gives the Commission a free hand only where the law is silent. Where the rules say the central government will notify Form 6, the Commission cannot change it at will. He says that for years he suggested the Commission use Aadhaar to catch duplicate entries, but the idea was put off citing privacy.

His view on the protests is measured. He accepts that the right of assembly is bound by reasonable restrictions of public order, but says the police commissioner should have opened talks with the organisers, as magistrates do in the districts. In his view, under Delhi's commissionerate system the same uniformed officer both issues the prohibitory order and enforces it.

The piece's most political claim is that the blame for lakhs of names being cut is now falling on the ruling party, and the BJP leadership must weigh whether keeping the Chief Election Commissioner in office is in the interest of the country and the party. His advice to voters: don't wait for the leaders, fill in Form 6 and save your vote.
nazar: When a former officer with long experience of running elections says the Commission's conditions are outside the law, it is hard to dismiss this as 'opposition politics'. But the advice to fill in Form 6 has its limits too: putting the burden of saving their names on those who lack a smartphone, papers and time only carries the same injustice further.
sawal: Is saving the vote the voter's responsibility or the Commission's?
ref: Article 326
The article of the Constitution that bases Lok Sabha and Assembly elections on adult suffrage. Every citizen aged 18 who has not been disqualified is entitled to be a voter.
Article 324
The article that gives the Election Commission the superintendence, direction and control of elections. Courts have held that this power fills gaps in the law, it does not override the law.

h: The referee in the dock: the government can win at the barricades, not trust
dek: According to an India Today investigation, in the fight over Gyanesh Kumar the opposition, the Cockroach Janata Party and the BJP are each playing their own game, and this tug of war will run long.
by: Kaushik Deka, Anilesh S. Mahajan, Avishek G. Dastidar
body: The magazine's long investigation begins with a basic difference. The CAA, farm laws and wrestlers' movements were against a law or a person, but this time the target is the referee of the game, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The writers argue that it is hard for the government to bend here, because admitting flaws in the voter roll would mean questioning its own mandate.

The spark was a 23 September report that two election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had recorded written objections 14 times to decisions linked to the SIR. In court, the movement is asking for the Commission's files, database access logs, booth-wise details of names cut, and an independent audit.

On 10 October, Cockroach Janata Party leaders were detained as soon as they reached Delhi, Jantar Mantar was sealed, dozens of metro stations were shut and mobile internet was cut. There is a wide gap between the police's and the petitioners' figures for how many people were detained. After this the group spread the movement across several cities, and 'Give us back our Jantar Mantar' became its slogan.

The report also catches the fine print of the relationships. The Congress openly treats these young people as allies, but privately fears that the group may one day become a party and its rival. In the BJP, meanwhile, the work is divided: Amit Shah defends the SIR with the 'infiltrators' argument, while the Prime Minister keeps himself out of the fight by staying silent.

The writers conclude that the government can win the street battle and keep the commissioner in office, but every closed road creates a new grievance. The Congress has an issue but a weak organisation; the young have energy but no concrete result yet. The final word will probably rest with the Supreme Court.
nazar: This investigation is no sympathiser of the movement, yet its most important conclusion is clear: the government has fewer answers and more arrangements. When the question is 'why was my name cut' and the answer is metro closures and internet cuts, the biggest loser is the poor voter who has no lawyer or platform.
sawal: If the referee himself is in question, who will heed his whistle?
ref: Article 324

The provision of the Constitution that gives the Election Commission the power to conduct elections. The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only by a process like that for a Supreme Court judge.
Form 6
The form filled in to become a new voter. Its changed declaration is a point of dispute between the Commission and the opposition.

h: A crack in the wall of fear: Ashok Vajpeyi hears change coming
dek: Senior poet Ashok Vajpeyi believes that young people have fearlessly laid the foundation of change, and that the courtier media will sink before the government does.
body: In his weekly column 'Kabhi-Kabhar' (Now and Then), Ashok Vajpeyi begins this time with a prophecy. In his view the present regime is sure to go, but before that the media that has been beating the regime's drum will collapse. He sees this as a hopeful stage in the repair of democracy, and says change can no longer be put off by repression, money or the old Hindu-Muslim debate.

The writer mentions the 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the Tricolour) event that the Cockroach Janata Party held at Connaught Place in Delhi on 16 October. According to him, thousands of security personnel were deployed to stop the flag being hoisted in Central Park, the park stayed closed for two days and many young people were detained. Vajpeyi is stung by the irony that even peacefully hoisting the national flag has become hard in the capital.

He stresses that every protest so far has been non-violent, and that this is the organisers' declared policy. The writer alleges that the grabbing, the use of force and the mistreatment of women came from the security forces or from people who came with their backing.

From this he draws two or three conclusions. First, despite its massive security apparatus, the government cannot stop the movement, not even by picking up leaders from their homes or airports. Second, the young are no longer scared by intimidation, and the structure of fear built up over years has cracked. Third, this fearlessness is slowly spreading to ordinary citizens, who can no longer be easily fooled with lies.

The rest of the column is about art, the search for the sacred and the poor state of art archives, but its political part records an elderly writer's hope, which he sees in the courage of the new generation.
nazar: Vajpeyi's hope carries a poet's enthusiasm, and it is worth remembering that less fear is not a victory in itself. But the heart of what he says is right: when even waving the tricolour needs permission, the question falls less on the protesters than on a system that is afraid of its own citizens.
sawal: Will the breaking of fear solve the question of the vote?
ref: Kabhi-Kabhar
Ashok Vajpeyi's long-running weekly column, in which he writes on literature, art and current politics.
Godi media
A common term used by critics for TV channels and newspapers that lean towards those in power (literally 'lap media').

h: Demanding a change of government is no crime, it is how democracy breathes
dek: The Wire Hindi argues that the BJP, by calling 'regime change' treason, is treating the government and the country as one, and forgetting its own history.
body: The row began when lawyer Prashant Bhushan said the movement against the SIR had become a fight to change the government, and that this is the democratic right of citizens. BJP leaders such as Rajnath Singh, Nitin Nabin and Sambit Patra then linked it to street anarchy, Bangladesh-style upheaval and foreign collusion. The article says this response is intellectually dishonest.

The first argument is simple: the Modi government and the Indian republic are not the same thing. The government is a temporary arrangement chosen by voters; the country is sovereign. Calling the wish to remove the present government anti-national really makes the ruling party the owner of the country.

The second argument comes from the Constitution. Under Article 75(3) the Council of Ministers is answerable to the Lok Sabha, and under Article 19 the right to speak, assemble and form associations continues between elections too. Winning an election gives the right to govern, not the right to demand silence from citizens. According to the article, an opposition that is not allowed to try to win power is no opposition at all.

The article calls one-sided Sudhanshu Trivedi's definition that change through elections is democracy but 'regime change' is conspiracy, because the BJP has offered no evidence of violence or conspiracy. Using a single phrase does not prove a foreign hand.

The sharpest part is about the BJP's own past. The article recalls that Advani called the UPA government illegitimate and demanded its resignation, that Modi gave the slogan of a Congress-free India in 2013, and that Jana Sangh leaders were on the streets during the JP movement to remove Indira Gandhi's government. What was democratic resistance then, how did it become conspiracy today?
nazar: This debate is not about words but about space. When criticism of the government is called an attack on the country, the first targets are those whose voices are already weak: Muslims, Dalits, students and voters whose names are missing from the roll. Dinkar's line 'Singhasan khali karo' (vacate the throne) has been part of the politics of free India; making it a crime sets a dangerous precedent.
sawal: Since when did criticising the government become criticising the country?
ref: Article 75(3)
The provision of the Constitution under which the Union Council of Ministers is collectively answerable to the Lok Sabha.
Sampoorna Kranti (Total Revolution)
Jayaprakash Narayan's movement of 1974-75, in which several parties, including the Jana Sangh, took to the streets against Indira Gandhi's government.

h: Is the next strike on Iran settled? The Gulf states hold the key
dek: Jeffrey Sachs and Sybil Fares argue that the US-Israel war on Iran has paused, not ended, and the surest way to stop it runs through the Arab states of the Gulf.
by: Jeffrey D. Sachs and Sybil Fares
body: According to economists Jeffrey Sachs and Sybil Fares, the US-Israel war on Iran that began on 28 February 2026 is now only in a pause. The big fighting has stopped, diplomacy is stuck, and both sides are preparing for the next round. The writers say neither Washington nor Tel Aviv wants peace.

They list the signs: US war secretary Pete Hegseth's visit to Israel, alleged plans for new strikes on Iran's petrochemical and nuclear sites, the naval blockade of Iranian ports passing a hundred days, and reports that there will be no strike before the US midterm election on 3 November. The writers read this as a war timetable. In September, Trump rejected Iran's proposal for a seven-day ceasefire, and before the election spoke of 'finishing the job' while backing Netanyahu.

The writers place this hostility in a long history: the 1953 coup against Mossadegh, American support for the Shah, help to Saddam in the Iran-Iraq war, decades of sanctions, and the US exit from the nuclear deal in 2018. In their reading, the US wants to keep its dominance amid declining power, and Israel wants military supremacy over the whole region.

Their most important argument is about the Gulf states. American bases did not give them security; instead, they made them targets. So the writers want the Gulf states to declare that their land and airspace will not be used for any new attack on Iran, and that ties with Israel will not be normalised until a Palestinian state is created.

They suggest turning the mediation of Qatar, Oman and Pakistan into a lasting regional security framework that includes Iran, the Gulf states, Egypt, Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan. It would rest on mutual non-aggression, freedom of navigation at sea, and a nuclear-free zone that would eventually include Israel as well.
nazar: For India this is no distant debate. Lakhs of Indian workers work in the Gulf, and every shock in Hormuz reaches here as the price of cooking gas and diesel. If the next round flares up, the first to be hurt will be the families whose livelihood depends on money sent from abroad.
The writers' suggestion is worth noting: security comes not from an outside power but from mutual trust among neighbours. South Asia should remember this lesson too.
sawal: Will the Gulf states refuse to give their land for war?
ref: Arab Peace Initiative
A 2002 Arab League proposal offering full normal relations with Israel in exchange for a Palestinian state on the 1967 borders.

h: Serbia's students: no leaders, no party, and a jolt to power
dek: Aleksandar Matković argues that Serbia's student movement achieved what opposition parties could not in a decade, and that students in Europe should learn from it.
body: According to the writer, the blow that President Aleksandar Vučić's government took in Serbia's latest election was dealt not by an opposition party but by students. The movement began in 2024 when the roof of the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad collapsed, killing 16 people. But the writer sees a deeper anger behind it: local corruption, insecure jobs and poor-quality work at foreign companies.

He says the movement's strength was its independence. The students did not side with domestic parties, nor with Russia, China, the European Union or the United States. In the writer's view, most opposition parties are small, run from the top and corruptible, so joining them would have weakened the movement.

The students occupied universities and ran things themselves: security, food, medicines and alternative classes. In March 2025 the writer saw general assemblies of three to four hundred students at a faculty in Novi Sad. Candidates too were chosen through collective interviews, old politicians were kept out, and women and men were given equal places on the list.

Now the student list is in talks to form a government, and the writer also lists the challenges. The movement's programme condemns the genocide in Gaza, while Serbia's arms exports to Israel rose from 3.3 million dollars in 2023 to 126 million dollars in 2025. In the writer's view, the new government must at least stop these exports. American right-wing influencers also jumped into the campaign in its final days.
The writer concludes that students in Belgium, France, Italy and Spain face the same economic pressures, and that by ignoring Serbia, Europe has missed a lesson.
nazar: Serbia's story is a reminder that young people's anger is not just sloganeering; it can take the shape of organisation and democratic methods. General assemblies, collective decisions and distance from parties are exactly the things power fears most.
But the real test is now: whether the ethics of the street reach the government's table. The new government's stand on arms exports will show how far the movement has kept its promise.
sawal: Can a leaderless movement also run a government?
ref: Novi Sad disaster
In November 2024 the concrete canopy of Novi Sad station in Serbia collapsed, killing 16 people, after which a student movement erupted across the country.

h: 'We don't work for war': a voice rises from the ports
dek: Siddhartha Chakravarty and Rahul Maganti argue that dockworkers' action at more than a hundred ports can show a way to fight both genocide and the crisis of capital.
body: On 30 October, seafarers and dockworkers stopped work at more than a hundred ports from northern Europe to South Asia, for two hours in some places and a full day in others. According to the writers, this began on 6 February at more than 20 Mediterranean ports, where war cargo was stopped and shipping companies had to change routes. In India, 15 ports are taking part, led by unions linked to CITU.

The writers connect this to dockworkers' long tradition of international solidarity: refusing to unload goods from apartheid South Africa, raising funds for strikers on other continents, and refusing to touch war cargo during the India-Pakistan wars of the 1960s. In February 2024 an Indian union announced a boycott of ships carrying ammunition to Israel, after which its offices were raided.

They say this is not only a moral question but also one of workers' lives. In 1944 an explosion on a ship loaded with war cargo at Bombay port killed more than a thousand workers. In 2026 alone, 64 seafarers have lost their lives in the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war.

The writers also list the changing conditions at ports. Permanent jobs at major ports fell by 67.4 per cent between 2012 and 2024, and by a further 18.5 per cent after that. More contract work and overtime have led to more accidents, and workers are now also demanding protection against automation.

Their larger argument is that capitalist crises often lead towards militarisation, as happened in the long depression of the nineteenth century and after 1929. Since 2008, the wars in Ukraine, Palestine and Sudan are signs of the crisis of that same old order, and dockworkers are pointing to an alternative.
nazar: When governments stay silent on war, the hands that carry the cargo speak up. The participation of 15 Indian ports shows that the labour movement here is still alive, even if permanent jobs have shrunk.

This action is also a reminder that workers' safety and the demand for peace are not separate. The system that pushes workers onto contracts is the same one that makes them stand among crates of explosives.
sawal: Can workers' refusal slow down a war?
ref: 1944 Bombay dock explosion
On 14 April 1944, the SS Fort Stikine, loaded with ammunition and cotton, caught fire and exploded at Bombay port, killing a large number of dockworkers and firefighters.

h: Death for ten Adivasis in Bastar: why the promise of peace rings hollow
dek: Rashi Agarwal argues that the death sentence for ten Adivasis in the Jhiram Ghati case leaves many questions, and that the High Court should set it aside.
body: In September, a special NIA court in Jagdalpur convicted ten Adivasis (indigenous people) of Bastar for the 2013 Jhiram Ghati attack and sentenced them to death. In that attack a Congress convoy was ambushed and 27 people were killed, including Mahendra Karma, Nand Kumar Patel and Vidya Charan Shukla. Most of the accused have been in jail for almost 12 years, and the sentence still awaits confirmation by the Chhattisgarh High Court.

According to JNU researcher Rashi Agarwal, the judgment itself records different roles: one took part in a meeting, another arranged food and supplies. Yet all were given the same sentence. Most of the testimony came from surrendered former Maoists, while none of the injured or eyewitnesses identified the accused in court, and no weapons were found on them.

She points out that the court accepted that villagers can be forced by Maoists to help, yet still concluded 'knowing participation'. Factors such as poverty, no previous crime, the possibility of reform and long imprisonment were set aside, the case was called 'rarest of rare', and the sentence came just eleven days after conviction.

She recalls the 1980 Bachan Singh judgment, which held life imprisonment to be the rule and the death penalty the exception. According to a 2016 study, 76 per cent of prisoners sentenced to death were from backward classes or minorities, and very few death sentences handed down by lower courts survived appeal.

She also says the investigation into the larger conspiracy behind the attack is still incomplete. In July 2026 the state home minister ordered a review of Maoist-linked cases in which no life was lost. Her demand is that the High Court set aside these sentences and that the cases of Adivasis held for long periods be reviewed.
nazar: Talk of peace in Bastar will be credible only when there is justice for the Adivasis crushed in the middle of this conflict. The same death sentence after twelve years in prison, though the roles differed, raises the question of whether the court saw a person or only a region.
The burden of the death penalty falls again and again on those who lack a good lawyer, money and a voice. This case is a mirror of that whole system.
sawal: Will peace come to Bastar by way of the gallows?
ref: Bachan Singh vs State of Punjab (1980)
The Supreme Court ruling that the death sentence should be given only in the 'rarest of rare' cases, and that the offender's circumstances must also be weighed.

h: Unsafe blood in Pakistan: children pay the price while institutions sleep
dek: Former health adviser Zafar Mirza argues that the root of infections spreading through blood transfusions in Pakistan is not lack of knowledge but institutions that do not work.
body: The article opens with the HIV outbreak among children in Taunsa tehsil of Dera Ghazi Khan district in Punjab. According to Zafar Mirza, a joint investigation found that blood transfusions and dirty needles played an equal part in the infections. Between December 2024 and April 2025, 120 children under 12 were infected, and the number later reached 331.

The writer points out that HIV is spreading fast in Pakistan and that its burden of hepatitis C is the highest in the world. Both are blood-borne diseases. The safe blood programme, started in 2010 with German help, built 17 regional blood centres, but after its national coordinator retired in 2020, no one was appointed.

He also lists the state of the provinces: Islamabad's authority is inactive, Punjab never framed the rules under its 2016 law, Sindh's rules are outdated, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's centres are underused, and Balochistan has neither staff nor money. His central point is that unsafe blood flows through useless institutions.

After Taunsa, a technical group was formed on the Prime Minister's intervention. Its recommendations include reviving the programme, activating the regulator in every province, replacing rapid kits in donor screening with modern tests, and building a national database of donors.

The writer believes intervention from the top helps but cannot take the place of strong institutions. He appeals to citizens, doctors and the media to demand accountability and to promote unpaid voluntary blood donation.
nazar: This story is not Pakistan's alone. In India too there have been reports of children infected through unsafe blood, and oversight of blood banks is weak. A poor family has no way to ask whether the blood being transfused has been tested.
The writer's point holds on both sides of the border: schemes are made on paper, but disease stops only when an institution does its job every day.
sawal: How much testing does your district's blood bank do?
ref: Taunsa HIV outbreak
The 2024-25 spread of HIV among hundreds of children in Dera Ghazi Khan district of Pakistani Punjab, blamed on unsafe blood and needles.

h: US midterms: how dangerous is Trump's 'October surprise'?
dek: Lawyer and author Steven Harper argues that his loosening grip on power has made Trump more dangerous than before, and the 3 November election is the test.
body: According to Steven Harper, who teaches law at Northwestern University, for Trump this election is not just about Congress but about escaping accountability. He argues that if the Democrats win a majority in either house, investigations into the use of power for private gain will begin, and it is this fear that makes Trump dangerous.

The writer lists Trump's troubles: a rift among supporters over the Epstein files, the Iran war, lifting sanctions on Russia and abandoning Ukraine, oil and diesel made costlier by the war, prices pushed up by tariffs, and record-low popularity. He also calls some cabinet members incompetent and accuses the administration of 'pay to play' corruption.

In Harper's view, the real 'October surprise' is not promises of cash payments or billions of dollars for farmers, but the fear of interference in the election. He says voter ID laws and arbitrary drawing of electoral districts may not be enough, and courts have already blocked orders to bring elections under federal control.

So election officials are training staff for situations such as the immigration agency ICE or other federal officers arriving at polling stations, ballots or machines being seized, as happened this year in Fulton County, Georgia, and the invoking of the Insurrection Act, which Trump has not ruled out.
The writer believes the courts fall behind Trump's pace. His conclusion is that the most reliable check is the voters themselves, and voting in large numbers is the answer.
nazar: That in one of the world's oldest constitutional democracies, election officials are preparing for federal agencies to arrive at polling stations is a warning in itself. When the person in power starts to see defeat as a threat to himself, every institution of the election comes under pressure.
The lesson for every democracy, India included, is that courts alone cannot protect elections. Aware and organised voters are the last guardians.
sawal: When power fears defeat, who will protect the vote?
ref: October surprise
A phrase in American politics: a sudden event or announcement in October, just before the November election, that can affect the result.
Insurrection Act
An 1807 US law that gives the President the power to deploy the military inside the country in case of rebellion or major unrest.

h: Five years in jail is enough: Khurram Parvez's bail stands
dek: The Supreme Court dismissed the NIA's plea against the bail of the Kashmiri human rights activist, citing his long imprisonment and the slow trial.
body: On Friday the Supreme Court dismissed the National Investigation Agency (NIA) petition challenging the bail granted to Kashmiri human rights activist Khurram Parvez. A bench of Justice M.M. Sundresh and Justice P.B. Varale refused to interfere with the Delhi High Court's order, and gave the accused's long imprisonment as the main reason.

Parvez was arrested in Srinagar in November 2021. The case concerns alleged terror funding under the UAPA. The NIA alleges that a network linked to Lashkar-e-Taiba recruited overground workers, gathered information on security installations and arranged money.

For the defence, senior advocate Tanveer Ahmed Mir told the court that Parvez walks with a prosthetic leg and has been in custody for nearly five years. He said even the framing of charges was delayed because in August the NIA asked for more time to file a supplementary chargesheet. Additional Solicitor General Raja Thakare appeared for the agency.

Earlier, in July, Justice Navin Chawla and Justice Ravinder Dudeja of the Delhi High Court had granted Parvez bail. The High Court based this on four and a half years in prison, the slow pace of the trial and the right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution. Now the top court has put its seal on that decision.
nazar: Under the UAPA bail has been made almost impossible, and the trial itself becomes the punishment. Khurram Parvez's case shows that even when the investigating agency delays the chargesheet, it is the accused who pays. The Supreme Court did the right thing, but the question is when this standard will reach the hundreds of other undertrial prisoners.
sawal: Five years in jail without a trial even starting: is that justice?
ref: UAPA
The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. Because of its Section 43D(5), bail becomes very hard to get if the charges look true at first sight.
Article 21
The fundamental right to life and personal liberty. Courts have also linked it to the right to a speedy trial.

h: Editor named 'accused' over dam protest violence: police seek search warrant against Tongam Rina
dek: Arunachal police have asked a court for warrants to search the homes of the editor of 'The Arunachal Times' and of the protesters' lawyer.
body: On 27 October the investigating officer of Pasighat police station applied to the Chief Judicial Magistrate of East Siang district for warrants to search the homes of four people. They are Tongam Rina, editor of 'The Arunachal Times', Sunny Tayeng, lawyer for the activists in custody, and two local youth leaders. The application calls all four 'accused', but cites no concrete evidence against Rina. The court has not yet passed any order.

The case is linked to the violence of 23 October that broke out in protest against the huge dam called the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project. An NHPC office was set on fire, police vehicles were burnt, and the homes of the BJP state president and two MLAs were vandalised. Anti-dam activist Ebo Mili says the protest was peaceful and things turned bad only when the police fired stun grenades and tear gas.

Rina says she felt disgusted but not surprised, because such threats are not new to her. She asked why the police went straight for a warrant without speaking to her or the lawyer, and alleged illegal surveillance. On 30 October the police spoke of a 'correction' over the phone, but gave nothing in writing.

Journalists' bodies in Arunachal condemned the violence in a joint statement, but questioned the inclusion of Rina's name and voiced fears that investigative powers were being misused. In 2012 Rina was shot outside her office, at a time when she had been criticising the dam plans. The attackers have never been caught.
nazar: Making a journalist who has raised questions about dams and Adivasi (indigenous) land for years an 'accused' in violence sends a message: reporting itself is now under suspicion. In Arunachal, frightening those who give the Adi community a voice, instead of listening to it, will only deepen the protest.
sawal: How did an editor who asked questions about a dam become a criminal?
ref: Siang Upper Multipurpose Project
A huge dam proposed on the Siang river in Arunachal. The local Adi community fears it will drown their villages, fields and identity.
BNSS Section 96
The provision of the new criminal procedure code under which a court can issue a warrant to search a place.

h: Fake account, real detention: Chennai economist picked up at 5 am
dek: MIDS professor A. Kalaiyarasan alleges police took him from his home without any papers over a post from a fake account that carried his photo.
body: A. Kalaiyarasan, associate professor at the Madras Institute of Development Studies (MIDS), has complained to the Tamil Nadu DGP that three policemen in plain clothes came to his home in Adyar at around five in the morning, took his phone and said they were taking him to a police station in Pammal. According to him, no complaint, FIR or any other paper was shown, and he was not even allowed to inform his family.

The hired car stood near Pallavaram for about 45 minutes while the policemen talked on the phone, and then they said they had been ordered to drop him back home. On the way back he was shown a screenshot of an Instagram account that carried his photo and had been used to post insulting remarks about TVK MLA J. Kamachi. Kalaiyarasan says the account is not his and the photo was probably lifted from a Harvard website.

At home a written statement was taken from him and his phone was returned at about 7:45. The professor said that though he was himself a victim of identity misuse, he was treated like a criminal. The incident came after a TV interview in which he had raised questions about price rise in the state and the government's attitude.

CPI(M) state secretary P. Shanmugam called it a sign of a police raj and said that if there was a complaint, the path of a summons or an inquiry should have been taken. The station's inspector denied harassment and said questioning was necessary because the account carried his name and photo.
nazar: Picking up an economist from his home at dawn on the basis of a single fake screenshot shows how meaningless procedure has become for the police. When experts are treated like this, ordinary people will think ten times before speaking in public debate, and perhaps that is the aim.
sawal: Is taking someone away without an FIR questioning, or a threat?
ref: MIDS
The Madras Institute of Development Studies in Chennai, a well-known institute for research on development and economics.
D.K. Basu guidelines
Supreme Court directions of 1997 under which police must state their identity and inform the family when taking someone into custody.

h: Jane Kaushik hits back at a plea to erase trans identity
dek: A women's group has asked the Supreme Court to end legal recognition of transgender people, which the community has called an attack on its very existence.
body: An organisation called Women's Declaration International India (WDII) has filed a petition in the Supreme Court seeking withdrawal of the legal recognition given to transgender people. According to the report, the petition also speaks of taking mistreatment of transgender people out of the ambit of crime, and its language has been widely criticised.

Transgender activist Jane Kaushik has called it a direct attack on her existence and identity. The petition cites her own case and calls her a 'biological male', which she called deeply insulting. Kaushik points out that in 2025 the Supreme Court recognised her as a trans woman in her case and upheld her identity certificate.

The petition claims that Kaushik faced embarrassment because of the discomfort of other women living in a women's hostel. According to Kaushik, this story is made up: neither did the school make such an argument nor did the court find anything of the kind. In fact she had faced transphobic mistreatment from the school's staff and students. She alleges that the petition is creating a false conflict between the rights of trans women and those of other women.

The petition has been filed through a big law firm that has described itself as trans-inclusive. Kaushik said it is neither the organisation's job nor its lawyers' to comment on her identity, and that no government or outside agenda can erase her. The report does not carry the side of the organisation or its lawyers.
nazar: Twelve years after the NALSA judgment, trans people's identity is still being dragged into court again and again. This shows that rights granted on paper do not become secure on the ground. Targeting another marginalised community in the name of protecting women is not feminism; it is the opposite.
sawal: How does erasing one person's identity protect someone else?
ref: NALSA vs Union of India (2014)
The Supreme Court judgment that recognised transgender people as a 'third gender' and upheld the right to decide one's own identity.
Jane Kaushik vs Union of India (2025)
The case in which the Supreme Court upheld the identity of trans teacher Jane Kaushik, who had faced discrimination in schools.

h: 19 reserved PhD seats missing at JNU, BAPSA sit-in enters sixth day
dek: Alleging that 15 ST and 4 SC seats were left empty, students are insisting that the vivas be stopped.
body: Over the 2026-27 PhD admissions at Jawaharlal Nehru University, the Birsa Ambedkar Phule Students' Association (BAPSA) has been on an indefinite sit-in at T-Point since 24 October. The group alleges that this time 15 ST (Scheduled Tribe) and 4 SC (Scheduled Caste) seats were not filled at all. On the sixth day of the protest BAPSA went with other progressive student groups to meet the administration, a day after students burnt an effigy of the administration.

According to BAPSA, the prospectus invited applications from three cycles of UGC-NET, but candidates from the June 2025 cycle were left out without any notice. The group also says that the administration had promised to set up a committee to look into the irregularities, yet went ahead and announced viva dates, which they call a broken promise.

According to figures collected by BAPSA, not once in the past ten years has the 15 percent SC quota or the 7.5 percent ST quota been filled, and the OBC and disability quotas have also repeatedly fallen short. The Mooknayak has made clear that it has not independently verified these figures. According to JNUSU councillor Komal Devi, the administration has stopped admissions in the NET category this cycle, but admissions in the JRF category were to begin from 30 October.

The students' demands include re-notifying the empty seats, bringing back the entrance exam JNUEE, ending the 100 percent weightage of the viva, implementing the Thorat Committee's recommendations and a caste census on campus. There has been no official statement from the administration.
nazar: When admission rests entirely on an interview, reservation stays on paper and seats are left empty with the line 'no suitable candidate found'. Added up year after year, this shortfall shuts out a whole generation of Dalit and Adivasi researchers.
sawal: Why has the quota not been filled even once in ten years?
ref: Thorat Committee
A committee set up in 2007 to probe discrimination against Dalit and Adivasi students at AIIMS. Its recommendations are seen as important on caste discrimination on campuses.
JNUEE
JNU's own entrance exam. PhD admissions now happen through NET-JRF and interviews instead.

h: Satyajit Ray film institute: six students expelled, now an FIR against a student leader
dek: Amid a month of tension at SRFTI in Kolkata, a case of assaulting the vice-chancellor has been filed against the students' union vice-president.
body: Kolkata's Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) has filed an FIR at Panchasayar police station against students' union vice-president Shubham Waydande, accusing him of assaulting the vice-chancellor. Nine sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita have been applied against him. Waydande is one of the six students expelled on 15 October: he for three semesters, and the other five for two semesters each.

The dispute began at the end of September, when students protested against an event of the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat, which the report describes as linked to the RSS. On 4 October a mob from outside raised slogans at the institute's gate, and there were reports of stone-pelting and students being injured.

Waydande says that on 15 October he and some fellow students were protesting peacefully outside the vice-chancellor's office; someone threw a stone at a window, but he does not know who. The students were asking why the administrative gates were shut, why facilities were not being provided and why the expelled students could not meet the registrar. He says they were only asking for their safety on campus and are being targeted for raising questions.

According to registrar Deepak Kumar, the action was taken over misbehaviour with the vice-chancellor, intimidation and vandalism, and a sudden torch march on 27 October created an atmosphere of fear. The institute says it respects the right to peaceful dissent. The students are still on a sit-in, and questions are being raised about the police presence on campus.
nazar: The very students who complained of an attack on campus by an outside mob are now facing expulsion and an FIR, a pattern now seen at several institutions. Turning students' union leaders into criminals in the name of discipline changes the campus from a place of debate into a place of surveillance.
sawal: Why are those who complained of an attack the ones in the dock?
ref: SRFTI
Kolkata's film and television training institute under the Union Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, named after Satyajit Ray.
Rustication
Removing a student from an institution for a fixed period, during which they are cut off from studies and campus facilities.

h: A kidney for a debt: the journey of a farmer from Minthur
dek: This part of a PARI series tells how pressure from moneylenders took a farmer from Chandrapur all the way to an operating theatre in Cambodia.
body: The story of Roshan Sadashiv Kule, a farmer from Minthur village in Maharashtra's Chandrapur district, is the second part of a PARI series investigating organ trafficking. According to the report, at five one morning in October 2023, three moneylenders came to his house with sticks and demanded Rs 16 lakh. There was nothing left to mortgage or sell.

It is alleged that one of the six moneylenders told him plainly to sell a kidney, or his family would be targeted. In November 2023 Roshan joined a 'kidney donor' group on Facebook and then reached a WhatsApp group, where a 'handler' kept pushing him. After about eight months of talks, the deal was fixed in June 2024 at Rs 8 lakh.

At home he said he had got a job abroad as a computer operator. His passport was made in Nagpur, then he reached Kolkata by bus and train, where he was kept in a hotel room with about eleven others and their phones were taken. From there he was taken to Cambodia, where the operation took place at the end of October 2024. About Rs 7.5 lakh came into the account of his wife Rohini. Roshan was left with a permanent scar and lifelong restrictions.

Through Roshan's statement the police reached about a dozen more 'donors'. An FIR was filed in November 2025, the main accused was caught in Solapur in January 2026, and a chargesheet of about six thousand pages was filed in March. Police allege that this gang arranged 30 to 35 illegal transplants in Cambodia, Trichy and Bengaluru, in which recipients were charged Rs 50 to 70 lakh and donors got Rs 5 to 8 lakh.

The report does not treat the case as only a crime story. It argues that village debt, unchecked moneylending and a trafficking network spread across borders are links in a single chain, whose weakest end is the farmer who has nothing left to sell but his own body.
nazar: When cheap bank credit does not reach the village, the moneylender does, and his recovery is not governed by any law. Roshan's story shows that the cost of the farm crisis is now being paid not just with land and jewellery but with the body.
Strict enforcement of moneylending laws and easy institutional credit for small farmers are as necessary to stop organ trafficking as police action.
sawal: Are the laws curbing moneylending really enforced in villages?
ref: Human organ transplant law
This 1994 law (THOTA) bans the buying and selling of organs. It provides for committees to approve transplants.

h: Bamboo, shells and coconut: a Philippine village fights floods
dek: In Pamarawan village on Manila Bay, a sea barrier built with natural methods has held back floods, but some fishers' livelihoods have paid the price.
body: Pamarawan village, on the northern shore of Manila Bay in the Philippines' Bulacan province, is part of Malolos city, but can be reached only by boat. Every year the southwest monsoon, known there as habagat, would flood the village. A concrete wall three to four metres high proved helpless against storm waves.

According to this Mongabay report, bamboo frames have now been put up over 14 hectares in front of the village, filled with waste shells packed in coconut-fibre nets. These frames break the force of the waves and trap silt, so that the seabed rises and mangroves can be planted there. The project, costing about 13 crore pesos, began in 2024 and is due to be completed this year.

Villagers say there has been no flood for about two years. In some places nearly 30 centimetres of silt has built up, floating rubbish in the water has decreased, and shrimp, crabs and shellfish have begun to return. According to Haskoning, the company that designed the project, 80 to 90 percent of the construction workers came from this village.

The report also shows the other side of the picture. The fish pens and shellfish farms of more than fifty people fell inside the project area, their income was taken away and only some of them got compensation. The mangroves have not yet been planted, and the claim that floods have stopped rests mostly on statements by villagers and officials, not on any independent monitoring.

The background matters too. Between 1990 and 2002 Bulacan lost more than half its mangroves, and an investigation is under way into a scam in flood control projects in the province. The company's head himself calls this a practical experiment, not a formula to be copied exactly, while the mayor of Malolos argues that concrete alone is not enough.
nazar: From the Sundarbans to the coasts of Odisha and Gujarat, India's answer to the sea is also often a concrete wall. Pamarawan shows that natural defences like mangroves and silt can last, provided the plan also counts the livelihoods of fishers whose work lies in that same water.
A climate protection project is just only when its burden is not placed on the shoulders of the poorest.
sawal: When plans are made to save a coast, who asks the fishers?
ref: Nature-based solutions
Ways of protecting against floods and erosion with natural systems such as mangroves, wetlands or shellfish reefs. The IUCN has set a global standard for them.
Habagat
The Philippine name for the southwest monsoon. Every year it brings heavy rain and floods to coastal areas.

h: Rehabilitation built from an ASHA worker's diary: Subaida's account from Wayanad
dek: Speaking to BehanBox, Subaida, an ASHA worker from Mundakkai, says her house-by-house records helped draw up the rehabilitation lists after the 2024 landslide, yet her own job is still insecure.
body: Subaida, 57, from Mundakkai ward in Wayanad's Meppadi panchayat, has been an ASHA (community health) worker since 2008. Speaking to journalist Liniya Babu she says that at first she earned at most Rs 500 a month, and the work was limited to keeping records of pregnant women and newborns. Now it also includes chlorination, dengue prevention, disease surveys, family planning advice and visits to palliative care patients.

In 2024 she was responsible for 265 houses in Mundakkai. The first landslide struck at around 1 am, and her own home was destroyed too. That same night Neeli, from the Paniya Adivasi (indigenous) community, called her from a relief camp. Subaida told her group to run to the other side, and everyone survived. ASHA workers carried most of the burden of washing and identifying bodies in the first fifteen days.

According to Subaida, the most reliable house-by-house information later was in the ASHA workers' diaries. Workers from Chooralmala, Mundakkai and Attamala wards spent about a year at the Kalpetta collectorate preparing the official death report and the lists of families eligible for the proposed township at Elstone Estate. Subaida's own family has moved twice.

The pay tells the opposite story. In October 2026 she gets an honorarium of Rs 12,000 and a fixed incentive of Rs 3,000. The rest comes in scraps of Rs 20 to Rs 600 for vaccinations, deliveries and visits, and only if she covers 100 houses a month. There is no fixed date of payment: this October the honorarium came but the incentive did not. She estimates that about half the ASHA workers there are single mothers whose homes run on this income.

She supported the indefinite strike ASHA workers began outside the State Secretariat in Thiruvananthapuram in February 2025. About a year after the disaster she had a heart attack. Even so, on her doctor's advice, she keeps working.
nazar: The figures the government uses after a disaster to hand out houses, compensation and township plots come from the diaries of women it still runs on scraps of honorarium and incentives. As the weather worsens, such disasters will grow in the hills and villages, and every time these workers will be in the front line.

Praise and pats on the back are not enough. A permanent job, pay on a fixed date and separate payment for disaster work for ASHA workers should be the basic condition of any serious rural health policy.
sawal: Why is the job of the woman whose diary built the rehabilitation not permanent?
ref: ASHA
Accredited Social Health Activist. Under the National Rural Health Mission, the link between the village and the health system, paid an honorarium and incentives rather than a salary.
Mundakkai-Chooralmala landslide
The landslide disaster in the Meppadi area of Wayanad in July 2024, which wiped out several settlements and took hundreds of lives.

h: Death at sea: US strikes on boats in the name of drugs
dek: This Al Jazeera Fault Lines film goes to the families of people killed in US strikes in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific, and asks who the dead really were.
body: Since September 2025 the US military has been striking boats in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean that it says are suspected of drug trafficking. According to the film, more than 220 people have been killed so far in more than sixty strikes. This roughly half-hour Al Jazeera Fault Lines film, 'Killing at Sea', released on 2 September 2026, sets out to find the faces behind these deaths.

The Trump administration calls the campaign 'Operation Southern Spear' and describes it as a war against 'narco-terrorism'. The film points out that the government has put out very little information: who the dead were, what the evidence against them was, and on what basis the targets were chosen. There are no clear answers to these questions.

At the centre of the film are three families and two bombings. Correspondent Josh Rushing's team goes to the relatives of those killed, to eyewitnesses and to physical evidence gathered on the ground. The journey stretches from fishing communities in the Caribbean to Washington, and the effort is to understand what life was really like for those who were called only 'traffickers' in official statements.

Through conversations with legal experts, the film raises three questions. Are these strikes legal? Have they really stopped the drug trade? And where is the accountability for those killed? Under international human rights law, killing a suspected criminal outright instead of arresting and trying them is considered an extrajudicial killing, and on this basis several human rights groups have been questioning these strikes.

The film's page lists countries such as the Bahamas, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Jamaica and Grenada as within its scope. This is a region where the sea is the livelihood of many families, and where the history of American military power is long and bitter.

The film's strength is its method. Against loud official claims, it tries to give each death a name, a home and a family. A war being fought far from most people's eyes, on the open sea, comes out here in the words of those who were left behind.
nazar: When someone can be killed by being called a 'terrorist', without a trial and without any evidence being shown, the rule of law ends first for the weakest. Boatmen and fishers of the Global South are the easiest targets of this war, because there is no one powerful to ask questions about their deaths.
In India the language of 'encounter' (a police shootout, often alleged to be staged) does the same job: first a label, then no need for evidence at all.
sawal: How long can death without trial be called war?
ref: Operation Southern Spear
The US military campaign against boats suspected of drug trafficking in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific. The Trump administration calls it a war against 'narco-terrorism'.
Extrajudicial killing
A killing by the state without any court process. International human rights law treats it as a violation of the right to life.

h: On Panahi's sentence: whose trust is an artist's voice?
dek: Suman Shekhar's essay on Sammukh starts from Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi's latest sentence, goes on to persecuted artists around the world, and asks how asking questions became a crime.
body: Suman Shekhar's essay opens with the memory of a song from the film 'Rockstar' in which the hero demands his rights and dignity in front of a crowd. According to the writer, the song voices the anger that rises when power feels people no longer fear it, and it begins to use laws made in the name of peace and order against those very people.

At the centre of the essay is Jafar Panahi. The writer says that on 28 October a court in Iran sentenced him to five years and one month in prison, and, citing his lawyer, also mentions seizure of property and a two-year ban on travel and social media. Despite a twenty-year ban on filmmaking in 2010, Panahi made 'This Is Not a Film' at home, turning the ban itself into his subject.

The essay then runs through a long list: Mohammad Rasoulof, who had to flee to Europe after being sentenced; Ai Weiwei, who collected the names of children killed in the Sichuan earthquake and was detained; Cuban artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara; Oscar Wilde, Salman Rushdie and Oleg Sentsov. From India there is M.F. Husain, who had to leave the country amid court cases and threats.

The writer accepts that every case is different and that disagreement over them is fair. But he argues that censorship today is not just a ban on a film; it is also freezing bank accounts, shutting accounts, blocking travel and pressuring institutions. On reports that the film 'Satluj' was removed from OTT platforms, he asks who decides what citizens may watch, and on what basis.
The essay ends on a poem by Gorakh Pandey, and on the conclusion that cameras can be stopped and books seized, but a society that stops asking questions loses a part of its freedom.
nazar: This essay reminds us that a ban on an artist is really a ban on the rights of the viewer and the reader. In India too, films, books and comedy shows bow before mobs and government pressure, and in that light Panahi's stubbornness is a lesson: making fear itself the subject is also resistance.
sawal: Can love of country and disagreement with the government go together?
ref: Jafar Panahi
Iranian filmmaker, director of 'Offside', 'Taxi Tehran' and 'It Was Just an Accident', who has faced prison and bans again and again.
Sammukh
A Hindi literary web magazine that publishes essays, stories, poems, translations and reviews.
photo_note: The last days of Shah Jahan

h: The story 'Vande Mataram': Ahmed, who wanted to be a soldier since childhood
dek: Musharraf Parvez's story on Sammukh steps into the row over Vande Mataram through the plain, simple tale of a Muslim boy who becomes a soldier and is martyred.
body: Sammukh has published young writer Musharraf Parvez's story 'Vande Mataram', and in an editorial note calls it a response to the recent controversies over this song. Rather than retell the story here, we describe its structure and mood; the full text can be read on the original page.

It begins in a classroom. Angry that the homework has not been done, the teacher asks the children what they will become when they grow up. One wants to be a nurse, another a doctor, another a scientist, but Ahmed says he will be a soldier. These scenes are light, and the mix of Hindi and English in the children's speech makes them real.

At home his mother is overjoyed at this dream, while his father wants his son to become a doctor. In the argument between them, the mother's insistence that a mother too has a say in her children's future stands out. Fifteen years later Ahmed leaves home to join the army, and the farewell scene is full of both pride and fear.

The last part is an encounter with terrorists in a desolate valley, where Kabir, Manoj, Sunny and Raju fight alongside Ahmed. The comrades are killed one by one, and the wounded Ahmed dies in Raju's arms, leaving a message for his mother.

The story is emotional and straightforward, with no experiments in craft. Its strength is its context: by placing a Muslim soldier among comrades of different faiths, it says that love for the country is not the property of any one community.
nazar: When Muslims are asked again and again to prove their loyalty, the very writing of such a story is a statement. But a question remains: why should anyone have to be martyred to prove their patriotism? Equal rights should come from being a citizen, not from passing some test.
sawal: Should any citizen have to prove their patriotism?
ref: Vande Mataram
A song by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, regarded as the national song, over which disputes keep arising about making its singing compulsory.

h: A letter to Jamia's vice-chancellor: hunger strike and closed doors
dek: Researcher Musharraf Parvez's open letter on Hindwi Bela asks why, instead of talking to students sitting in protest for a students' union election, the campus was turned into a garrison.
body: In Hindwi's Bela section, Musharraf Parvez, a researcher at Jamia Millia Islamia, has written a letter to the vice-chancellor. The letter does not name the vice-chancellor, and what it records is the writer's own account. According to him, students have been on hunger strike for thirteen days, and all they ask is the right to vote in a students' union election.

The writer recalls that on Ambedkar Jayanti, in the M.A. Ansari Auditorium, the vice-chancellor had said he was always with the students. Now, the writer alleges, instead of talking to the students he came out with security staff, and students' phones were snatched by force. The writer calls this gap between word and deed what literature calls irony.

According to the letter, walls were raised in front of the gates, the campus was filled with police and online classes were announced, though many students have no internet at all. The writer gives the example of Aligarh Muslim University, where a similar issue was resolved, and of JNU, where the vice-chancellor comes from and where elections are being held.

The most concrete worry is about fellowships. Researchers have to mark attendance and sign in, but with entry blocked this is not possible. The writer says many students come from homes where one month's fellowship being stopped means the kitchen fire going out.

The last part of the letter is a personal appeal: the vice-chancellor should reflect alone; the university belongs to the students, and the vice-chancellor is a tenant here who will one day change. The writer's conclusion is sharp: the vice-chancellor stands not with the students but with an ideology.
nazar: A students' union is democracy's first school. If students at a central university must go on hunger strike to demand a vote and get walls and police in reply, this is not just Jamia's problem. The burden of stopped fellowships falls first on poor and first-generation researchers.
sawal: Should students at a university have to ask for the right to vote?
ref: Students' union election
The process of choosing student representatives at universities. According to the writer, these elections have not been held at Jamia for a long time.
Bela
Hindwi's prose section, which publishes essays, letters, memoirs and commentary.

h: A second visit to jail: Sarju, Babban and the forgotten boys
dek: The second part of Anuradha Sharma's memoir on Hindwi Bela listens, during a government project, to the stories of young men in jail for whom neither a lawyer nor family comes.
body: Anuradha Sharma is writing a memoir on Hindwi called 'Meri Pehli Jail-Yatra' (My First Trip to Jail). She is not a prisoner; she goes to the jail with her boss for a government project that involves working with prisoners. The second part begins on the night she decides, using a headache as an excuse, not to go the next day, and then, finding herself refreshed in the morning, sets off.

While waiting in the jailer's room, news comes in: one boy jumped from the wall and broke his leg, another has come back after trying to escape twice. Sarju, who works in the kitchen, brings tea. When the writer asks, he says he likes being at home, and that he did nothing. A guard tells her that more than eighty percent of the prisoners are poor and unlettered, and that many have had their cases hanging for years.

As Sarju tells it, a friend gave him a lift on a scooter, police stopped them at a checkpoint and the charge of theft fell on him. According to the guard, the real thief was the friend, no lawyer came for Sarju, and some NGO workers have filed a plea for his release.

The heaviest moment belongs to sixteen-year-old Babban, who has been locked up for three years. He talks about hitting a thief with an iron rod one night, and then begs the writer to get a message to his family, because no one has come to see him in three years and he fears he will forget their faces.

The part ends with the restlessness after returning from the jail. Even the work of transliterating Urdu into Hindi, which the writer loved, starts to feel dull, and the night passes with the faces of those boys.
nazar: This memoir is a reminder of the undertrial prisoners, who far outnumber convicts in India's jails. Bail and free legal aid exist on paper, but do not reach poor young men like Sarju. Minors being locked up for years is a question for the whole system.
sawal: Who is responsible for young men held in jail for years without a lawyer?
ref: Undertrial prisoners
People whose cases are still going on and who have not yet been found guilty, yet are in jail.

h: Obscenity in whose eye? A new writer's letter in reply
dek: Rudrani Priyadarshini's first published piece, on Hindwi Bela, is a letter to Viyogini Thakur that asks whether shame and obscenity lie in the body or in the mind of the one looking.
body: Hindwi's Bela section has published a letter by Rudrani Priyadarshini of Muzaffarpur, which, according to her introduction, is her first published work. The letter is a reply to Viyogini Thakur's essay 'Ashleel Sthitiyon Mein Phansna' (Getting Caught in Obscene Situations), in which Thakur wrote about some of her experiences. Rudrani does not reject that essay; she wants to take its questions further.

The first episode is about a girl who laughs on seeing animals mating, while Thakur is embarrassed. Rudrani argues that this is part of the cycle of life; the shame lies not in it but in the way of looking. A woman staring at an ultrasound centre, as if one goes there only for a pregnancy check, is in her view prejudice and lack of knowledge. She asks why we should not talk instead of looking away.

Her sharpest criticism is of doctors. One made guesses about her age and private life in the middle of an examination; another linked pimples to sexual desire and went so far as to advise marriage. According to Rudrani, these are less examples of ignorance than of a social outlook that people absorb so deeply that they take it for the truth.

The letter's main point is that the real obscenity is forcing one's prejudices on others, and that these people are products of the same system. That does not excuse their behaviour, but merely blaming individuals leaves the root untouched.

Finally Rudrani puts her finger on a remark of Thakur's own, which guesses that the girl who laughed must by now be married with children. Her question is whether the prejudices we want to free others from are not also sitting inside us in some other form.
nazar: This letter matters because a very young voice directly challenges the policing of women's bodies by society, doctors and family, and puts herself in the dock too. For girls in small towns, even a health check-up is surrounded by shame and questions; this is directly a matter of their health.
sawal: Does shame lie in the body, or in the eye of the one looking?
ref: Letter series
The open letters now appearing on Hindwi Bela, in which writers raise public questions while addressing a particular person.

h: A promised review, a debt to Gandhi: an honest refusal before writing
dek: Manish Kumar Maurya's letter on Hindwi Bela apologises to a translator that, though he has read her book on Gandhi, he cannot yet review it, and explains how much work a true review demands.
body: Manish Kumar Maurya's letter is addressed to Kalpana Shastri, who translated Chandrakant Wankhede's Marathi book into Hindi as 'Gandhi Kyon Nahin Marte!' (Why Gandhi Does Not Die!). According to the letter, she bought copies of the book with her own money, brought them to a Gandhi camp and asked readers to write and send their opinions. Manish had promised to write a review.

Before reaching the book, the letter takes an amusing detour. Manish tells the tale of his postman, who read a letter containing an unfinished story and kept asking for its ending for two days. This brings to mind the yaksha of Kalidasa's 'Meghaduta' (The Cloud Messenger), whose private message the whole world read. This part makes the letter light and warm.

Then comes an account of the camp: on what terms the book was handed out, and how a senior colleague, Antaryami Maharana, bought a copy for him. Manish says he could not find any detailed review of this book, available in Hindi for four years, and so he wanted to write one.

But after reading the book his conclusion is the opposite: for now he can write neither on this book nor on Gandhi. His argument is that a good review means going to each of the author's sources, testing how the evidence is used and catching what is left out or repeated, and in the case of a translation the original Marathi should be looked at too. By his reckoning this could take years.
The letter postpones the promise; it does not break it. Manish writes that he will not stay away from Gandhi, and whenever he sees attacks on Gandhi, he will try to answer them in Gandhi's own words.
nazar: In an age of quick opinions and instant reviews, this letter makes the case for patient reading. The attacks on Gandhi today can be answered not with slogans but by reading Gandhi carefully.
sawal: Is a review written without reading deeply a betrayal of the reader?
ref: Gandhi Kyon Nahin Marte!
Kalpana Shastri's Hindi translation of Chandrakant Wankhede's Marathi book.
Meghaduta
Kalidasa's poem in which an exiled yaksha (a celestial being) sends a message to his beloved through a cloud.
